newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa urged to privatise telecom sector faster.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa urged to privatise telecom sector faster.

text.p: The accelerated privatisation of all telecommunications services was vital if South Africa wanted to keep abreast of international developments in information technology, two University of Cape Town academics said in an article punlished on Monday.

James Hodge and Jonathan Miller said in the latest edition of UCT's Trade and Industry Monitor that the decision to partially privatise Telkom but give it a five year exclusivity period could affect the development of other information infrastructures.

"For instance, the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research's community information delivery system based on wireless technology has run into problems with Telkom when attempting to move beyond the pilot stage," they said.
The present arrangement also did not provide a level playing field in all services.
"An example is the role of Telkom as a network provider and Internet service provider, which has already led to allegations of unfair competition through hidden subsidies," the authors said.

Telkom responded to allegations by asking the South African Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (SATRA) to classify Internet access as a basic service, which would have allowed it to continue providing the service regardless of the outcome of Competition Board investigations. This application failed.
These developments highlight the need for government to adopt a regulatory environment that allowed for the rapid growth of all telecommunications networks, Hodge and Miller said.

They said that while the financial services and retail sectors appeared to be making the most effective use of information technology (IT), manufacturing was lagging behind and needed to get up to speed if it was to become internationally competitive.

"At all levels of government in South Africa, the country suffers from a high level of inefficiency and ineffectiveness, partly resulting from historical structures but certainly exacerbated by very poor IT," they said.
This highlights the need to encourage and promote the use of IT in small to medium sized enterprises, traditionally low-tech sectors and parts of the public sector.
Given the low level of computer literacy in South Africa, especially among blacks, the professional training and education of IT users would also be important, Hodge and Miller said.
